Trying to Conceive

Preconception Health: How to Prepare Your Body for Pregnancy

Updated: July 1, 2026

This article is shown in English while its translation is prepared.

The months before you start trying can matter just as much as pregnancy itself. Preparing your body early gives a baby the healthiest possible foundation and can make conceiving smoother. Here is a clear, practical checklist to work through.

Start a prenatal vitamin with folic acid

Begin taking a daily prenatal vitamin containing folic acid ideally two to three months before you try to conceive. Adequate folic acid in the earliest weeks — often before you know you are pregnant — significantly lowers the risk of neural tube defects.

Look for a prenatal that also includes iron, iodine, and vitamin D, and confirm the right dose with your healthcare provider, since some people need more.

Book a preconception check-up

A visit with your doctor before pregnancy is one of the most valuable steps. It is a chance to review your medical history, current medications, family history, vaccinations, and any chronic conditions such as diabetes, thyroid issues, or high blood pressure that are best stabilized beforehand.

Ask which of your medications and supplements are safe to continue, and whether any screening or vaccines (like rubella) should be updated first.

Nourish your body

Aim for a balanced, whole-food diet: plenty of vegetables and fruit, whole grains, lean protein, healthy fats, and calcium and iron-rich foods. There is no single "fertility diet," but overall nutrition supports hormonal balance and a healthy weight.

Reaching a healthy weight range before pregnancy can improve fertility and reduce risks, so small, sustainable changes now are worthwhile.

Adjust lifestyle habits

Stop smoking and avoid alcohol and recreational drugs, which affect both fertility and early development. Keep caffeine moderate.

Prioritize sleep, gentle regular exercise, and stress management. Chronic stress and exhaustion can affect cycles, and building good routines now makes the transition into pregnancy easier.

Prepare your mind and your calendar

Learning how your menstrual cycle works helps you identify your fertile window once you begin trying. It also helps to talk openly with your partner about timing, expectations, and support.

Give yourself grace: for most healthy couples conception can take several months, and that is completely normal.

Key takeaways

  • Start a folic-acid prenatal vitamin 2–3 months before trying.
  • Book a preconception check-up to review medications, conditions, and vaccines.
  • Eat a balanced diet and aim for a healthy weight range.
  • Stop smoking, avoid alcohol, and moderate caffeine.
  • Learn your cycle and be patient — conception often takes a few months.

Frequently asked questions

How far in advance should I start preparing?

Aim to begin about three months ahead, mainly so folic acid levels build up before the earliest weeks of pregnancy. Even a few weeks of preparation is better than none.

Does my partner need to prepare too?

Yes. Sperm take roughly three months to develop, so a partner improving diet, limiting alcohol, and avoiding smoking during that window supports healthier sperm.

Do I need to stop birth control early?

Fertility usually returns quickly after stopping most methods, though cycles can take a little time to settle. Your provider can advise based on the method you use.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
